what_it_does: When a chip design is translated into an actual network of logic gates (called a gate-level netlist), engineers need tools that can automatically recognize higher-level patterns — for instance, spotting that a cluster of gates implements a full adder (a circuit that adds two binary numbers). This pattern recognition underlies both chip verification (checking the design is correct) and logic optimization. The problem is that standard recognition methods rely on structural matching: they look for an exact arrangement of gates, and any rearrangement caused by earlier optimization steps breaks the match. BoolE attacks this by using a technique called equality saturation, which exhaustively explores many logically equivalent ways to express the same Boolean function and stores them all at once in a compact data structure called an e-graph. A custom extraction algorithm then searches this rich structure to find high-level components that would be invisible to rigid structural matching.
